And the paper validates the proposed method on two datasets and shows better prediction and label privacy protection compared to existing models.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Strength 
- The paper studies an interesting and essential problem.
- The claims of the paper are well-supported via experiments.
- The proposed method shows improved results on two public datasets.

## Weaknesses.
From my perspective, I have several concerns which I will detail below:
- This the generative model conditional? I understand that the method is trained with a step of reconstruction. In this case, it should be a conditional generative model. If so, it might be better to clarify it to avoid confusion. Meantime, I'm wondering about the idea behind the reconstruction step. Is that important to separate the reconstruction (step 2) and generator training (Step 3)?
-  I'm not sure if I misunderstand the experiments, I feel that the paper overclaims a bit about the improvement. From experimental results, I feel like the improvement is actually very marginal.  For table 1, the improvement is only +1% is kinda marginal to me.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: From my viewpoint, the paper is of high clarity, quality, and novelty. I'm not sure about the reproducibility because I'm not an expert in federated learning.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper is addressing an interesting and essential problem. At the same time, I would like to hear back from the authors during the rebuttal just in case I misunderstand anything.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This work proposes a method for a particular federated learning setup where separate agents have access each to their own data and not the labels (client/passive models) and one agent has access to labels of the data (server/active model), and the challenge is to train a model at the server without leaking labels to potential attackers listening to the gradient back-propagation from server to client models. The proposed method archives this by minimizing the divergence between the distributions of clients’ predictions (output of clients) and true labels (with additive noise), while at the same time minimizing the cross-entropy loss between the true label and the transformed (decoded) clients’ predictions within the server. This makes sure the clients’ predictions are noisy enough that their gradients are not easily separable into classes, while informative enough that the decoder can extract the correct label from them. The experiments on two relatively simple datasets, using one client and one server, shows promising results in maintaining predictive performance while not leaking labels compared to baseline SplitNN classifier and naive noise addition as in Marvell.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**

The paper reads well, and is clear for the most part (there are some missing explanations I’ll get to later). The proposed method is novel and interesting, and shows promising results on small experiments.

**Weaknesses**

I have the following concerns/questions about the paper:

1) The explanation of why the method works is not substantial enough in my opinion, I’d suggest adding more discussion on how each part of the loss contributes to the performance vs leakage rather than merely introducing what they individually do.

2) To me it seems like the additive noise in Eq.2 is doing much more than claimed in the paper: “continuous support and not too concentrated in the space”. It is the very reason why your method works! As I understand it, the GAN loss makes sure the predictions’ distribution is close to a zero-centered normal distribution – the larger the sigma the more the addition of Y is negligible – and hence not very informative of the labels, while the subsequent decoder together with the reconstruction loss makes sure this distribution is not completely uninformative of the labels. In essence, seems to me you are optimizing a VAE where the KL term of the ELBO is modeled with the GAN loss, and the reconstruction term is modeled with, well, the reconstruction loss. There is already evidence for this in your paper, where increasing the sigma of the additive noise (hence closer to zero-centered normal in the KL sense) improves protection (bottom of page 7). So, I’d like to see this discussion included in the paper (the point I mentioned above as well), as well as two closely related experiments: First, what if instead of Y+noise only noise is used? (this I believe should work, if not, the reasons must be discussed) Second, what if a VAE formulation is used? (this is an easy extension of what you currently have and sheds light on the role of GAN, that is, the fact that the whole loss is actually a VAE ELBO).

3) The experiments with one client seems too restrictive to me, in the sense that an important feature of federated learning is the presence of many many clients with their local data, so a more realistic setup of multiple clients and one server should also be considered, and the effect of an increase in the number of clients on the protection must be studied. I suspect as the number of clients increase, it becomes more challenging to make their predictions all look similar yet maintain predictive performance. But then again, increasing the capacity of the decoder can help overcome this – another direction that also needs to be explored.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is well-written and easy to follow in my opinion, and except for the lack of some more in-depth technical discussions I mentioned above, the overall problem statement and solution is clearly explained. The proposed method is novel as far as I know, and sufficient details are provided for reproducibility.

**Typo fixes and Unclear Statements**

Unclear sentence Page 1: “In VFL, the data is vertically partitioned and participants whose datasets share the same sample space but differ in feature space”

Page 1: HFL is mentioned but is not defined.

Page 2: “GAFM framework offers better protection data.”

Page 2: “which have been used by the HFL.”

Page 3: “for label protection in VFL.”

Page 4: The following statement is false, see [1, 2] below: “Wasserstein distance-based GAN can improve the stability of learning and get rid of problems such as pattern collapse”

Page 6: “Spambase and Credit datasets”

Page 9: “Marvell”

[1] Fedus, William, et al. "Many paths to equilibrium: GANs do not need to decrease a divergence at every step." ICLR (2018).

[2] Mescheder, Lars, Andreas Geiger, and Sebastian Nowozin. "Which training methods for GANs do actually converge?" ICML (2018).
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper studies a specific setup of the federated learning where data and label are owned by different agents, and the label owner seeks to train a classifier without leaking the labels in the process, and without directly accessing the data. The proposed method is novel and seems to work in restricted experiments, but I think some in-depth discussion of the role of each part of the proposed method is missing, as well as more realistic experiment settings (as detailed above).
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes using GAN to reduce label leakage in vertical split learning, by maximizing GAN loss while simultaneously minimizing the classifier loss. Paper uses WGAN to conduct experiments.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Weaknesses:
1. The paper is written in a way thats very complicated to understand. I had to read the previous paper Li et al to understand Marvell method mentioned multiple times in the paper to actually get the basic idea
2. The paper lacks a lot of detail around different split models, i.e. the various neural network components that will be needed to be implemented to actually implement the paper. In short - I am not confident if a third party can actually reproduce/implement the paper 
3. The paper doesn't do rigorous testing on benchmarks, no image datasets are considered, Different architectures are not considered either
4. The paper adds a lot of math - in middle of paragraphs - so its even harder to follow the chain of thought that author has.
5. Paper has typos (run a spell check, grammar check please)
6. Paper uses Leaky AUC as the only measure of leakage - not the information theoretic bounds studied when discussing differential privacy
content.summary_of_the_review: while this could be a good idea and a good paper - in its current state I found paper can use a lot of work.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
